lessons.words: dwelling – a house where people live; disciple – pupil, follower; anxious – troubled mentally; exile – living outside one's own country; Durvasa – a great sage; Yudhishtira – first of the Pandavas in the Mahabharata; mound – raised ground; hooted – shouted; ill-treat – show discourtesy; ragged – dressed in torn clothes; hospitality – friendly reception of guests; mansion – a grand house/palace; astonished – wondered; tribe – people; lily – a flower; bloom – open, blossom; exceeding – great; writest – write; thou – you; vision – seeing someone/something; accord – grant, agree, bring into harmony; cheerly – cheerfully; thee – you; fellow man – another human being; vanished – disappeared; wakening light – light which rouses from sleep/in active condition; blest – blessed; lo! – a word used for calling attention; legit – lawful
lessons.notes: Unit 5 has a prose lesson 'The Wonder Bowl' (p. 1–11) and a poem 'Abou Ben Adhem' by Leigh Hunt (p. 12–17). Theme: Generosity. Story: the old couple Philemon and Baucis welcome two ragged strangers (angels) with the little they have; their kindness is rewarded – the milk bowl never empties and their cottage becomes a mansion. Language: (1) Adverbs describe how an action is done (finely, angrily, loudly); adjectives describe nouns (ragged, palatial). Adverb → 'with + noun': carefully – with care. (2) Suffixes: joy–joyful, dictate–dictation, hope–hopeful, comfort–comfortable. (3) Homophones (words that sound alike but are spelt differently): peace–piece, principal–principle, dairy–diary, weak–week, dear–deer. (4) Simile: comparison of two different things using 'as' or 'like' (like a lily in bloom). Teacher note: the book spells 'Yudhisthira' (p. 2) but 'Yudhishtira' elsewhere; p. 17 'He born on October 19, 1784' should be 'He was born on October 19, 1784'.
ab: Before You Read – Look at the picture and listen to the story (p. 1–2)
1. Who gave the Akshaya Pathra to Yudhishtira?
Lord Surya gave the Akshaya Pathra to Yudhishtira.
2. What was special about the Akshaya Pathra?
It gave unlimited food till Draupadi finished her meal.
3. Who arrived in the house of the Pandavas?
Sage Durvasa and his disciples arrived in the house of the Pandavas.
4. What was Yudhisthira worried about?
He was worried because there was no food left to serve the sage and his disciples, since Draupadi had already finished her meal.
5. When did Draupadi pray for help?
Draupadi prayed to Lord Krishna for help when there was no food left, while the sage and his disciples were bathing in the river and were about to return for their meal.
6. How did Krishna satisfy Durvasa and his disciples?
Krishna found a single grain of rice in the Akshaya Pathra and ate it. His satisfaction made Durvasa and all his disciples feel so fully fed that they never came to Yudhishtira's house.
7. Discuss how, from an unknown quarter, help arrives when it is needed the most.

Check your understanding – C1 Answer the following in a word, a phrase or a sentence each (p. 3)
1. Which sentence in the first paragraph shows that Philemon and Baucis were poor?
"They worked hard in their farm and were only able to get as much food as they needed."
2. Would any stranger who came to their house go without food?
No, they would never let any stranger who came to their door go without food.
3. Why did the dogs bark?
The dogs barked because two ragged strangers had come to the village and the village boys were hooting at them.
4. What made Philemon say that the boys were bad?
The boys hooted at the poor strangers and ill-treated them, so Philemon said that the boys were bad.
Check your understanding (p. 4)
1. Why did Baucis feel that the strangers should have come earlier?
Baucis had only a small bowl of milk to give them. She felt that if they had come a little earlier, they could have shared the couple's supper.
2. What were the strangers pleased with?
The strangers were pleased with the kindness and hospitality of Baucis and Philemon.
3. What made Baucis astonished?
Baucis was astonished when the strangers filled their cups again and again from the bowl, because there had hardly been a drop of milk left in it.
4. Together, the couple decided that the strangers were ________. (fill in the blank with the right word)

Think about the text – C2 Discuss with your partner/group and write the answers (p. 7)
1. Describe the hospitality of the old couple picking out at least two examples.

The old couple never let any stranger go without food. They welcomed the guests with joy and shared their own meal with them. Philemon drove away the dogs and took the ragged strangers into the cottage, and Baucis gave them the only thing she had – a small bowl of milk.
2. What makes Baucis think that the strangers were not ordinary people?
Baucis saw that the bowl, which had hardly a drop of milk, was filled again and again as much as the guests wanted. So she thought that they were not ordinary people.
3. What did the strangers tell Philemon and his wife before going away?

They said, "We are God's messengers. We are much pleased with your kindness. Ask for anything you like. You shall have it!" Later they told the couple to live in the mansion as long as they desired and to come to heaven together.
Think about the text – C3 Discuss the answers with your teacher (p. 7)
1. Would Philemon and Baucis treat any other strangers in the same way?
Yes. They were kind by nature and never let any stranger go without food. They would treat every stranger who came to their door with the same love and hospitality.
2. Why did God's messengers come to the village?

God's messengers came to the village to find out who was kind and hospitable. All the villagers except the old couple ill-treated them. So they rewarded Philemon and Baucis for their kindness. (ಶಿಕ್ಷಕರೊಂದಿಗೆ ಚರ್ಚಿಸಿ ಸೂಚಿತ ಉತ್ತರ)
Think about the text – C4 Read the following extracts and answer the questions (p. 7)
1. "Don't worry, good lady" – a. Which lesson is this line taken from?

1. b. Who is the "lady"?
The "lady" is Baucis, the wife of Philemon.
1. c. When did the speaker say so?
The guest said so when Baucis felt sorry that she had only a small bowl of milk to offer and wished they had come earlier.
2. "May your bowl be full of milk always" – a. Who said this?
The guests (God's messengers / the angels) said this.
2. b. Who did he say this to?
He said this to Baucis (and Philemon), the old couple.
2. c. Why did the speaker say so?
He said so to thank the couple for their kindness and hospitality and to bless them.
3. "Good angels, we wish to die together" – a. Who does the word 'we' refer to?
'We' refers to Philemon and Baucis, the old couple.
3. b. Who was it said to?
It was said to the angels (God's messengers).
3. c. Why did the speaker say so?
The old couple loved each other so much that neither wished to live without the other, so Philemon asked that both of them should die together.

Poem – Abou Ben Adhem: Before You Read – Edward Tells the Truth (p. 12)
A. A boy takes Edward's lunch money, then threatens to hurt Edward if he tells anyone what happened. What is Edward likely to do?
Edward is likely to tell a teacher or his parents about it, because he always tells the truth and believes that honesty is more important than fear. (ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.)
B. Edward's best friend Aaron steals a book from the school library, but regrets it and returns the book. He asks Edward not to tell the librarian. What is Edward likely to do?

Edward is likely to advise Aaron to tell the librarian himself. He will not tell a lie if he is asked, because he feels that telling the truth is more important. (ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.)

Poem – Abou Ben Adhem: C2 Rearrange the sentences so as to form a summary of the poem (p. 15–16)
Rearrange the sentences a, b, c, d to form a summary of the poem.

ಸರಿಯಾದ ಕ್ರಮ: c → a → d → b
c. One night Abou Ben Adhem woke from a deep, peaceful dream. In the moonlight that was making his room as bright as a beautiful flower, he saw an angel writing in a book of gold.
a. The peaceful sleep had given Ben Adhem courage, and he asked the angel: 'What are you writing?' The vision looked up and, with a sweet and friendly look, answered: 'I am writing the names of all the people who love the Lord.'
d. 'And is mine one of those names?' asked Abou. 'No, it is not,' replied the angel. Abou, still cheerful, spoke more softly and said: 'Then please put my name down as one that loves other people.'
b. The angel wrote, and vanished. The next night the angel came again, in a great flash of light, and showed the names of those who had been blessed by the love of God. And look! Ben Adhem's name was at the top of the list.

2. The rhyming words in the poem have a pattern. It is  a. every two lines rhyme  b. alternate lines rhyme  c. all lines end in the same sound
a. every two lines rhyme (e.g., room – bloom; gold – bold; said – head; Lord – accord)
3. The poem refers to God's representative in three different ways. They are:  a. moonlight, angel and dream  b. angel, the presence, the vision  c. lily, angel and dream

Poem – Abou Ben Adhem: C4 In your own words write the message the poem gives (p. 17)

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. ಸೂಚಿತ: Loving our fellow human beings is the best way of loving God. God loves and blesses those who love and serve other people.
Poem – Abou Ben Adhem: Know your poet (p. 17)
Know your poet: Leigh Hunt

Leigh Hunt, in full James Henry Leigh Hunt, was an English critic, essayist, poet and writer. He was born on October 19, 1784 at Southgate, Middlesex, England and died on August 28, 1859 at Putney, London.

lessons.au: ಸಮಿತಿ ರಚನೆ (Prose); Laura Howell Horner (Poem – Mountain Climbing)
lessons.words: modest – small; rebellious – one who fights against something / to resist; snow clad – covered with snow; amuse – feel pleasantly happy; persuade – make someone believe; graduation – getting a degree; mentor – adviser, guide (ಮಾರ್ಗದರ್ಶಕ); determination – decisive (ನಿರ್ಧಾರಿತ); adventure – exciting or dangerous experience, journey; mountaineering – the sport or activity of climbing mountains (ಪರ್ವತಾರೋಹಣ); avalanche – a mass of snow, ice and rocks falling rapidly down a mountainside; summit – top of the mountain; mist – a cloud of moisture in the air; eager – full of interest; assent – climbing up/movement; stumble – walk unsteadily; tackling – dealing with a difficult task; numb – not able to feel or move; incline – a slope; fascinate – attract; apex – highest point, peak
lessons.notes: Unit 6 has a prose lesson 'Journey to the Top' (p. 18–29) on Bachendri Pal, the first Indian woman to climb Mt. Everest (23 May 1984, 1:07 p.m.), and a poem 'Mountain Climbing' by Laura Howell Horner (p. 30–33). Theme: Courage. Language: (1) Relative pronouns / conjunctions join two parts of a sentence – who, which, where, why, what (He settled near Uttarkashi where he got married; Her graduation thrilled her parents who wanted her to be the first girl with a degree). (2) Prefixes un-, in-, dis-, im- give the opposite meaning (active–inactive, dependent–independent, expected–unexpected, honour–dishonour, employed–unemployed, experienced–inexperienced, complete–incomplete). The listening text on p. 74–75 (Saalumarada Thimmakka, Sudha Chandran, Kiran Bedi, Sania Mirza) is answered in the Listening Text lesson as well.

Check your understanding – C1 Answer in a word, a phrase or a sentence as required (p. 21)
1. What amused the family of Bachendri Pal?
Her dream of flying in aeroplanes and meeting famous people amused her family.
2. Where was Bachendri Pal born?
Bachendri Pal was born at Nakuri, a small village in the Garhwal Himalayas in the present Uttarakhand.
3. Where did Bachendri Pal apply for her Basic Mountaineering Course?
She applied to the Nehru Institute of Mountaineering (NIM), Uttarkashi.
4. Who was Brigadier Gyan Singh?
He was the Director of the National Adventure Foundation (NAF) and Bachendri's mentor.
5. For what purpose was the 'Bhagirathi Seven Sisters Adventure Club' established?
It was established to help poor girls and women use their mountaineering skills to make a living.
Check your understanding (p. 23)

She was selected for the Indian Everest Expedition of 1984.
2. What is the Nepali name for the highest peak in the world?

3. Which is the country's highest sports award that was given to Bachendri?

4. Name the autobiography of Bachendri Pal.

Check your understanding – C2 Answer each question and compare with your partner (p. 24–25)
1. Describe the trade of Bachendri Pal's father.
Her father was a border tradesman. He took wheat flour and rice from India to Tibet on mules, horses and goats and traded them.
2. Write about Bachendri's love for adventure and the mountains.

Bachendri was a rebellious child who loved wandering in the snow-clad Garhwal Himalayas. At the age of twelve she climbed 4000 m with her classmates. This experience increased her love for adventure and the mountains. Later she joined the Nehru Institute of Mountaineering, completed her courses with flying colours and climbed Gangotri and Rudugaria.
3. Why did Bachendri apply to NIM for a course?
In spite of her degrees, she got only temporary and junior-level job offers. Inspired by her love for the mountains, she decided to apply to NIM for the Basic Mountaineering Course.
4. Name the awards given to Bachendri Pal.

The Arjuna Award, 'Padmashri', the National Adventure Award, the 'Yash Bharathi' award (Government of Uttar Pradesh), the 'Gold Medal' of the Indian Mountaineering Foundation, an award from the Department of Education, Uttar Pradesh, and the Lifetime Achievement Award by the Kolkata Sports Journalists Association.
5. As students, what do we learn from Bachendri Pal's life?
ಸೂಚಿತ ಉತ್ತರ: We learn that hard work, determination and the will to succeed can take us to great heights, even if we come from a poor background.

lessons.notes: Unit 7 has a prose lesson 'Nest with Grandparents' by Lalitha Sridhar (p. 34–47) and a poem 'Dear Grandma and Grandpa' (p. 48–50). Theme: Love for grandparents. Story: Anjali, an only child, resents giving up her room for her grandparents (Dada and Dadi), but slowly learns to love them; when they leave she misses them and calls them back. Language: (1) Kinship terms – siblings, paternal grandfather (father's father), maternal grandmother (mother's mother), cousin, nephew, niece, aunt, uncle. (2) Prepositions show the position of an object: in, on, under, near, inside, outside, between, at, above, below; more: of, to, from, against, with, during, for. (3) Abstract nouns / hidden words and crossword with words from the lesson. Rhyme: 'two' rhymes with 'you' in the poem.

2. What made the family feel awkward with the arrival of the grandparents?

3. Pick out two examples from the eighth paragraph to show that the grandparents objected to their habits.

2. They thought pop music was 'noise' and ice-creams were 'not good for health'. (Also: they would not go to restaurants or watch movies in theatres.)

Anjali felt as if she had been suddenly imprisoned and that the house looked too small.

Dadi took over the kitchen because she was bored of doing nothing. She was a fantastic cook and served divine parathas, subzi, mithai, pakoras, salads and pickles. Anjali's mother could slow down, rest her feet and spend more time with her daughter, and she was satisfied that her child was in caring hands.

lessons.notes: Unit 8 has a play 'Wealth and Values' (p. 51–63) about the rich businessman Mr. Balaji and his sons Gagan and Rahul, and a poem 'The Quarrel' by Eleanor Farjeon (p. 64–68). Theme: Forgiveness. Message: money alone cannot bring happiness; 'To err is human, to forgive is divine'; 'In forgiveness there is happiness and peace.' Language: (1) Present continuous tense – is/am/are + verb-ing (The baby is drinking milk; I am writing my notes). (2) Plurals: name–names, cow–cows, sheep–sheep, wolf–wolves, fox–foxes. (3) Adjectives describe or give information about a noun or pronoun (large city, great king, ripe mangoes). (4) Hidden words, opposites (happy–sad, rich–poor, takes–gives, enemies–friends). Poem – The Quarrel: C3 Discuss the following with your partner and answer (p. 66)
1. How do you understand the lines seven and eight?

Lines seven and eight are "He said he was right, / I knew he was wrong!" Each brother thought that he himself was right and the other was wrong. Because neither would accept his mistake, the quarrel became stronger.
2. "We hated one another" – says one of them. Is it true? Why do you think so?

ಸೂಚಿತ ಉತ್ತರ: It was true only for that moment. They were so angry that they felt hatred, but it did not last long. Soon the brother apologised and they were friends again, because they really loved each other.
3. What message does the poem give?
Quarrels often start over small things and grow big. We should not go on quarrelling; we should accept our mistake, say sorry and forgive quickly.

2. Discuss the end of the quarrel.

Suddenly the brother thumped the poet on the back in a friendly way and said, "Oh, come on! We can't go on all night – I was in the wrong." By accepting his mistake, he ended the quarrel and they became friends again.

Poem – The Quarrel: Know your poet (p. 68)
Know your poet: Eleanor Farjeon

Eleanor Farjeon was born in London in 1881. She wrote children's stories and fantasy stories and soon became popular with both children and adults. She lived in Sussex, UK and was a personal friend of War Poet Edward Thomas and his wife Helen. The Farjeon Award is awarded periodically for an outstanding work in children's literature.

lessons.words: Epimetheus – a boy in the story; Mercury – the messenger (of the gods) wearing a winged cap; Pandora – the beautiful girl; companion – a friend who is with you; weary – very tired; stagger – walk unsteadily; curious – eager to know; coax – persuade gently; glittering – shining brightly; beseech – beg; wounds – injuries; dainty – small and delicate; Hope – the good fairy who came out of the box
lessons.notes: Supplementary reading (p. 69–71). Epimetheus and Pandora live happily until Mercury leaves a mysterious box with them. Pandora's curiosity makes her open it; ugly stinging creatures (sorrow and pain) fly out and spread in the world, but the fairy Hope comes out last and heals the wounds. Moral: curiosity without thinking can bring trouble; hope never leaves us. The next supplementary reading, 'A Birthday Present – Nehru to his Daughter' (p. 72–73), is a letter written by Jawaharlal Nehru from Naini prison on 26 October 1930 to Indira Priyadarshini on her thirteenth birthday. It advises her that the best way to find truth is by talking and discussing, and that she should never think she has learnt everything. The book gives NO exercise for this letter, so no answers are added.
ab: Pandora's Box – Check your understanding (p. 71)
1. What harm did Pandora bring through her curiosity?

Out of curiosity Pandora opened the lid of the box, and all kinds of ugly stinging creatures flew out. They stung Epimetheus and Pandora and then flew out of the window and spread sorrow and pain everywhere in the world.
2. Who helped to cure those who were hurt?
A dainty fairy called Hope helped to cure those who were hurt. She came out of the box, touched gently the wounds of both the children and flew out into the world to do the same for others.
